questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) What is the main function of the ALU and the Internal bus in a processor?

(b) State and explain TWO stages of the instruction cycle carried out in the control unit of the CPU. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) ALU and internal bus**

- The **ALU (arithmetic and logic unit)** carries out the **arithmetic operations** (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and the **logical operations** (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons) on the data held in the registers; the result is put in the accumulator or another register.
- The **internal bus** is the set of wires **inside the processor** that **carries data, addresses and control signals** between the registers, the ALU and the control unit.

**(b) Two stages of the instruction cycle (2 marks)**

1. **Fetch.** The control unit copies the address held in the **program counter (PC)** into the **memory address register (MAR)**, the instruction at that address is read from memory into the **memory data register (MDR)** and then into the **instruction register (IR)**, and the PC is **incremented** to point to the next instruction.
2. **Decode.** The control unit **decodes the instruction in the IR** (it separates the operation code from the operand/address) to know which operation must be done and which circuits to activate.

(The third stage, **execute**, then carries out the operation, using the ALU if needed, and the cycle repeats.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
A school intends to create a LAN of 10 computers.

(a) Describe each of the following network topologies by making a labeled diagrams:

- Star. (1 mark)
- Ring. (1 mark)
- Bus. (1 mark)

(b) Name and explain TWO aspects to consider when selecting a network topology. (2 marks)

(b) Explain TWO major advantages of using a wireless LAN instead of a cable LAN. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) The three topologies (3 marks)**

**Star.** Every computer is connected by its **own cable to a central device (hub or switch)**, which relays the data to the destination. If one cable fails only that computer is cut off, but if the central device fails the whole network stops.

```text
  PC1   PC2   PC3
    \    |    /
     \   |   /
   [ HUB / SWITCH ]  <- central device
     /   |   \
    /    |    \
  PC4   PC5   Server   (10 computers in all)
```

**Ring.** Each computer is connected to **exactly two neighbours**, so the cable forms a **closed loop**; the data travel **in one direction** from node to node (often controlled by a token) until they reach the destination. A break in the ring can stop the network.

```text
      PC1 ---------> PC2
     ^                  |
     |                  v
    PC10               PC3
     ^                  |
     |                  v
    PC9                PC4      ... (PC5 to PC8 continue the loop)
```

**Bus.** All the computers are connected to **one main cable (the bus or backbone)** shared by everybody, with a **terminator at each end** to stop signal reflection. The data are sent along the cable and each computer reads the data addressed to it. It is cheap and easy to extend, but a break in the backbone stops the network and collisions increase with the traffic.

```text
 PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4        PC10
  |     |     |     |    ...    |
==+=====+=====+=====+===========+==   backbone (bus) cable
[T]                              [T]   T = terminator
```

**(b), first - Two aspects to consider when choosing a topology (2 marks)**

- **Cost**: the length of cable and the number of devices (a star needs more cable and a switch; a bus needs the least cable).
- **Reliability / fault tolerance**: what happens when a cable or a device fails (in a star only one machine is lost; in a bus or a ring a fault can stop everybody).
- (Also acceptable: **ease of installation, troubleshooting and expansion** when computers are added, **performance** under heavy traffic, the **size** of the building and security.)

**(b), second - Two advantages of a wireless LAN over a cable LAN (2 marks)**

- **Mobility and flexibility**: users can move around the school with laptops, tablets or phones and stay connected; no computer is tied to a socket.
- **No cabling**: it is **cheaper and quicker to install** (no trenches, ducts or sockets), it is **easy to add new devices** and it can be used in buildings where cabling is difficult. (Another acceptable point: visitors can be given access easily.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Describe the following programming concepts.

(a) Compilers. (2 marks)

(b) Interpreters. (2 marks)

(c) Variables. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Compiler (2 marks)**

A compiler is a translator program that **translates the whole source program (high-level language) into machine code (object code) in one go**, before the program is run. It **reports all the syntax errors** found, and when there are none it produces an **executable file** that can be run again and again **without the compiler or the source code**, and that runs **fast**. (Examples: C, Pascal.)

**(b) Interpreter (2 marks)**

An interpreter **translates and executes the source program one statement at a time**, with **no object code kept**. It **stops at the first error**, which makes **debugging easy**, but the program **runs more slowly** because every statement is translated again each time it is run, and the interpreter and the source code must be present. (Examples: BASIC, Python, JavaScript.)

**(c) Variable (2 marks)**

A variable is a **named storage location in the memory** that **holds a value that can change while the program runs**. It has a **name (identifier)**, a **data type** (integer, real, character, string, Boolean) and a **value**; it is declared at the start of the program or procedure. Example: in Pascal `age : integer;` then `age := 17;`.
